title: What Is Rethymno Like?
seoTitle: What Is Rethymno Like? The Town, Honestly Described
seoDescription: A working Cretan city of about 30,000 with a Venetian-Ottoman old town, a 12 km beach and a university - what it feels like, hour by hour and season by season.
summary: Rethymno is a working Cretan city of roughly 30,000 people rather than a resort, built around a Venetian and Ottoman old town that you can cross on foot in about fifteen minutes, with a sixteenth-century fortress on the hill above it, a small fishing harbour, and a sandy beach running east for some twelve kilometres. Because the University of Crete's humanities campus is here, several thousand students live in the town, which keeps ordinary cafes, bookshops and restaurants open all year and stops the centre feeling seasonal. The old town is dense, shaded and largely pedestrian, with wooden Ottoman balconies overhanging narrow lanes; the beachfront strip east of it is generic package-holiday architecture and feels like a different place. The pace is slow, lunch is long, and almost nothing important happens before ten in the morning.
body:
## The short answer

Rethymno feels like a small Cretan city that happens to have tourists in it, rather than a resort that happens to have Cretans in it. That distinction is the whole character of the place.

## The four Rethymnos

The town divides cleanly into parts that feel nothing like each other.

**The old town** is the reason to come. Venetian street plan, Ottoman overlay: narrow lanes, wooden upper storeys projecting over your head, doorways with carved Venetian lintels, bougainvillea, and the occasional minaret above the roofline. It is dense and shaded, which matters in August, and largely closed to traffic, which matters always. Souliou Street is the narrow shopping lane everyone photographs; Ethnikis Antistaseos is the market street where the town actually buys things. The Rimondi Fountain, dated 1626, sits in a small square in the middle and still runs.

**The Fortezza** occupies the Paleokastro hill at the north-west corner - a Venetian fortress built between 1573 and 1580, largely emptied of its buildings but with intact ramparts. It is a shell, and the point of going up is the walk around the walls and the view down over terracotta roofs to open sea. In summer it hosts the Renaissance Festival, which is the best use anyone has found for it.

**The beach and the strip** run east from the old harbour: sand, shallow water, and behind it a coast road lined with large hotels, car-hire desks and restaurants with laminated menus in six languages. This stretch, out towards Platanes and Adele, is ordinary package-holiday Crete. It is not unpleasant, but nobody would describe it as Rethymno.

**The new town and the university** sit above and behind, and this is where the town lives - apartment blocks, a hospital, supermarkets, the University of Crete's humanities and social-sciences campus on the hill. Several thousand students give the town a completely different texture from a purely seasonal resort.

## What a day feels like

Mornings start late. Shops open around nine, the market street fills, and the old town is cool and quiet enough to walk properly. By eleven the day-trip coaches have arrived and the main lanes are busy.

Between two and five the town more or less stops. Lunch is long, shops close, and the heat pushes everyone indoors or into the sea. This is not a slogan - it is a scheduling fact, and planning around it saves a lot of frustration.

From six the old town refills, this time with locals as well as visitors. Sunset is the best hour: the Fortezza walls and the harbour mole both catch it, and the light on the Venetian stone is the thing photographers come for. Dinner starts around nine and runs late; the bar streets in the old town are loud until two or three in the morning in July and August, which is worth knowing before you book a room on one of them.

## Season by season

| Season | What it is like |
| --- | --- |
| April-May | Green, mild, quiet. Wildflowers inland, sea still cold. Best month for walking |
| June | Warm, busy but not yet full, sea comfortable. Arguably the best all-round month |
| July-August | Hot, crowded and loud in the old town; the beach strip at capacity; everything open |
| September-October | Warm sea, thinning crowds, harvest under way inland. The other best window |
| November-March | Rain, wind, closed beach hotels - but the old town keeps working because of the students. Carnival, one of the largest in Greece, falls in late winter |

## The texture of the place

- **It is walkable and hostile to cars.** The old town lanes are barely wide enough for a vehicle and much of it is restricted. Park at the edge - there are paid lots near the harbour and along the seafront - and walk.
- **It is not expensive.** Food, coffee and accommodation all price below Chania, and well below Santorini or Mykonos.
- **English is widespread**, and so are German, and increasingly French and Italian, in anything tourist-facing.
- **The mountains are always visible.** Psiloritis, at 2,456 metres the highest point in Crete, rises to the south-east; the White Mountains sit to the west. The town is never more than forty minutes from serious terrain.
- **The sea is on the north side**, which means it catches the north wind. When it blows, the beach is choppy and the south coast is the better swim.
- **Cats.** A great many, mostly fed, entirely unbothered by you.

## What Rethymno is not

It is not a luxury destination, and it is not trying to be. There are no cliff-edge infinity pools of the kind the Cyclades sell. The old town has good small hotels rather than grand ones. The harbour front is pretty but the restaurants on it are the weakest food in the city - the good places are one street back, or out in the villages.

It is also not a quiet place in August. If you want silence in high summer, stay in a village inland or on the south coast and come into town for the evening.

## Who tends to like it

People who want a real town rather than a resort; people who want to walk everywhere; people using Crete as a touring base; returning visitors who have already done Chania and Santorini and want somewhere they can settle into. People who want everything laid on within a single hotel complex tend to prefer the strip east of town, and to see very little of the place described above.

faqs.a: It is a working Cretan city of about 30,000 people, not a resort. The centre is a dense Venetian and Ottoman old town of narrow, largely pedestrian lanes under wooden overhanging balconies, with a sixteenth-century fortress on the hill and a small fishing harbour below it. A sandy beach runs east from the harbour, and behind that the ordinary town - apartments, a hospital, a university campus - carries on regardless of the season.

Parts of it are. The harbour-front restaurants and the hotel strip east along the coast are firmly tourist territory. The old town lanes one street back, the market street and the new town are not - they are where the residents shop and eat, and the several thousand university students keep it that way.

In July and August, yes - specific streets in the old town run bars until two or three in the morning. It is very localised, so the practical advice is to check which lane a room is on before booking. Outside those two months the old town is quiet by midnight.

Very. The old town crosses in about fifteen minutes on foot, the beach starts at its eastern edge, and the Fortezza is a short climb at the western end. Driving inside the old town is close to impossible and largely restricted - park at the edge and walk.

faqs.q: What is Rethymno like in winter?
faqs.a: Wet, windy and much quieter, with the beachfront hotels closed. The old town keeps going because of the university, so the cafes, bookshops and year-round tavernas stay open, and the Carnival in late winter is one of the biggest in Greece. It feels like a Greek provincial city rather than a holiday town, which some people prefer.

Yes. The beach is sandy with shallow entry, the old town is pedestrian and small enough that children cannot get far, and the day trips within reach - Lake Kournas, the Imbros gorge walk, the south-coast beaches - are all manageable in half a day or less.
